l3sd-intro: Short Deck (6+ Hold'em) is a popular poker variant played with 36 cards (6-A), with 2, 3, 4, and 5 removed. This creates significantly different game dynamics: more flops, more draws, and more action.
Short Deck is hugely popular in Asian high-stakes games and the Triton series. Compared with standard hold'em it has higher variance but more action.

1. Deck: 36 cards (6-A), 2-5 removed
2. Hand-ranking changes (two flips vs standard hold'em):
   - Trips > straights (standard hold'em: straights > trips)
   - Flushes > full houses (standard hold'em: full houses > flushes)
3. Smallest straight: A-6-7-8-9 (Ace low for the smallest straight)
4. Ante structure: usually no blinds — everyone posts an ante plus the BTN posts an extra ante

Short-deck hand rankings (weak to strong):

1. High card
2. One pair
3. Two pair
4. Straight
5. Trips
6. Full house
7. Flush
8. Four of a kind
9. Straight flush
10. Royal flush

Compared with standard hold'em, the relative positions of straights/trips and full houses/flushes are swapped.

The easiest mistake: treating trips as near-nuts and betting heavy. In short deck trips only beat straights — they lose to full houses and flushes, so on wet boards you must fear the opponent's stronger made hands.

1. Hand-value changes:
• Pocket pairs and big high cards (AA/KK/QQ/AK) rise in relative value; AK is the strongest non-pair starting hand
• Small pairs drop in set-mining value — trips rank below full houses/flushes, so implied odds worsen
• Suited connectors (JTs, 98s, etc.) play well with plenty of draw opportunities, but they aren't top tier — don't treat them as "roughly standard hold'em AKs"
• Flush value rises significantly — in short deck a flush beats a full house

2. Higher flop rate:
• 36 cards make it easier to hit the flop

3. More draws and action:
• Straight draws are more common
• Pots are usually bigger (ante structure + more calls)
• Variance is higher, so bankroll management must be more conservative

Short deck has only 9 cards per suit, so draw outs must be recalculated:

- Flush-draw outs = 9 − seen cards of that suit. Example: holding 2 hearts with 2 hearts on board → flush outs = 9 − 4 = 5 (standard hold'em would be 13 − 4 = 9)
- The 2/4 rule still roughly estimates equity, but the outs base must be on 36 cards — directly using the standard hold'em outs table systematically overestimates equity

The key to Short Deck is understanding the simultaneous changes in hand rankings and hand values. Standard hold'em's "standard plays" can be serious errors in short deck. Practice at low-stakes short-deck tables first, adapting to the ranking changes and range adjustments before moving up.
l3sd-cbet: Short-Deck C-Bets: High Frequency on Dry, Big Sizes on Wet

The basic logic of the short-deck continuation bet (C-Bet) is the same as standard hold'em, with two short-deck-specific adjustments: (1) on dry high boards (like K♠7♦2♣) you can C-Bet at high frequency — the opponent rarely hits and a small bet steals or bets thin value; (2) on wet connected boards (like 9♦8♣3♥) short-deck draw density is high, so you must protect with big sizes rather than small bets.

Short-deck C-Bet rule: dry boards 1/3 pot at high frequency (about 70%+); wet boards 2/3+ pot at low frequency (about 30-40%). On wet boards small bets give draws too cheap a price, and short-deck draws get there easily — protect with big bets.
High Frequency on Dry vs Big Sizes on Wet

On dry high boards (like A♠9♦2♣) the raiser's range dominates and the opponent rarely hits — use 1/3-pot small bets at high frequency to make the wide-range weak hands fold or bet thin value. On wet connected boards (like 9♦8♣3♥, 6♦7♣5♥) short-deck straight/draw combo density is extremely high, the raiser's nut advantage drops, C-Bet frequency falls to 30-40%, and you use 2/3+ pot big bets to protect overpairs and strong made hands, charging the draws.

Example: Short deck, you (BTN) open and the BB calls; flop K♠7♦2♣ (dry). You're the aggressor with plenty of Kx and the opponent rarely hits a K. Use 1/3-pot small bets at high frequency: KQ/KJ bet thin value, A-high semi-bluffs, small pairs also bet — the whole range pressures and the BB's weak hands fold.

Example 2 (big size on wet): Same pot, flop 9♦8♣3♥. The BB's defense range holds plenty of 9x/8x/draws and the nut advantage tilts to the BB. You hold K♠K♦ (overpair): still ahead but easily outdrawn by straights/two pair — use a 2/3+ pot big bet (pot 6, bet 4+) to protect and charge the straight/flush draws, not a cheap price. A-high and small pairs should check for pot control.

Counterintuitive point: small C-Bets on wet short-deck boards are an error. Because draw density is high and draws get there easily, a small bet gives draws too cheap a price — effectively a free chase. On wet boards you must protect made hands with big sizes; small bets are only right on dry boards.

Short-deck C-Bet quick memory: dry boards 1/3 pot at high frequency; wet boards 2/3+ pot at low frequency. First judge board wetness — the more connected and wet, the lower the C-Bet frequency and the bigger the size.
l3sd-donk: Short-Deck Donk: Rare But Powerful Leads

A donk bet is an OOP player betting first postflop before the opponent bets. In standard hold'em the donk is usually an error (giving up the check-raise lever, range imbalance); in short deck the donk is still rare (about 3%-5%) but on specific boards (where OOP's range dominates and nut combos are dense) it's reasonable or even optimal. Short-deck flop rates are high and draw density large, so the donk's protection and value-bet meaning is amplified.

Short-deck donk rule: only use it on specific boards where "OOP's range clearly dominates and nut combos are dense" (e.g. OOP has high two-pair/straight density in a limp pot). Otherwise default to checking to keep the x/r lever.
When to Donk and the Risks

Two short-deck donk timings: (1) boards favoring OOP's range — when the OOP defense range holds more two-pair/straight/flush combos, lead to protect equity; (2) wet-board protection — OOP hits strong and donks to charge the opponent's draws. Risk: the donk range is naturally strong, can't balance when raised, and gives up the x/r lever. So the donk is an exception, not the norm.

Example: Short deck, you (BB) call a BTN open; flop 6♠7♦4♣ (wet connected). You hold 7♠8♠ (middle pair + straight draw); your defense range has plenty of 6x/7x/8x and straight draws — nut combos dense. The BTN (IP) mostly has big cards that miss here. You donk half pot: protecting your middle pair/draw and making the BTN's big cards fold or pay. OOP's range dominates this board, so the donk is reasonable.

Example 2 (donk risk): Short deck, you (BB) call and flop A♠K♦2♣ (dry high). The IP BTN's range holds plenty of Ax/Kx and your OOP range is at a disadvantage. If you donk, you're torn when raised and give up the x/r. Correct play is checking and letting the BTN bet before you decide. OOP is at a range disadvantage on dry boards — donking is an error.

Counterintuitive point: the short-deck donk isn't a universal "aggressive protection" tool but a specific "board ownership" choice. It's reasonable when OOP's range dominates, otherwise check to keep the x/r. Mindless donking advertises range imbalance for free.

Short-deck donk three questions: (1) does OOP's range dominate this board? (2) can I handle being raised after my donk? (3) is checking to keep the x/r better? Only donk when the range dominates and draw density is high; otherwise check.
l3sd-check-raise: The check-raise (x/r) is one of the OOP player's most important postflop levers, especially in short deck: because draw density is high and opponents C-Bet frequently, the short-deck OOP builds a polarized x/r range of strong made hands + strong draws, suppressing the opponent's betting frequency and protecting the check-call range. The value of the short-deck x/r semi-bluff is amplified by the high value of made draws.

Short-deck x/r rule: the x/r range consists of strong made hands (nut pairs/two pair/straights/flushes) + strong draws (flush/straight draws), polarized. Use semi-bluff x/rs that retain improvement room when called.
The Math and Application of the x/r

Short-deck x/r semi-bluff break-even (pot P, opponent C-Bet B, your raise R):

EV(x/r) = f×P − (1−f)×[(1−E_win)×R − E_win×(P+R)]
(f = opponent fold rate vs x/r, E_win = equity when called)

Example: pot 6, opponent C-Bets 2, you x/r to 6; fold rate 50%, your straight-draw equity when called 35%:
EV = 0.5×6 − 0.5×[0.65×6 − 0.35×(6+6)] = 3 − 0.5×[3.9 − 4.2] = 3 + 0.15 = 3.15

The short-deck semi-bluff x/r EV is higher because made draws (flushes/straights) carry great value. (Concept from: Short Deck Poker x/r and semi-bluffs)

Short-deck x/r applications: on wet boards (high draw density) where OOP's range dominates, x/r semi-bluff with straight/flush draws; on dry boards x/r strong made hands for value. The x/r both protects your draws and makes the opponent's wide-range C-Bets pay.

Example: Short deck, you (BB) call a BTN open; flop 9♦7♣3♠. You hold 8♠9♠ (top pair + straight draw). BTN C-Bets 2 ante, you x/r to 6 ante. If he folds you win the 8 ante pot directly; if called you have top pair + straight-draw improvement room. On wet short-deck boards the x/r semi-bluff protects your marginal made hand while suppressing the BTN's C-Bet frequency.

Example 2 (dry-board x/r): Short-deck flop A♠K♦2♣, you (BB) hold 22 (set). BTN C-Bets and you x/r for value — his range has plenty of Ax/Kx that will call your set's value bet. Short-deck sets aren't the nuts (lose to full houses/flushes), but on a dry board they're strong and the x/r value bet is sound.

Counterintuitive point: the short-deck x/r isn't "fighting back with strong hands" but "building a polarized range". It must include both strong made hands and strong-draw semi-bluffs, or the opponent will figure out that your x/r is only nuts and fold, or only draws and call.

Short-deck x/r three questions: (1) is my x/r range polarized? (strong made + strong draws) (2) is the opponent's C-Bet frequency high? (if so, the x/r is more effective) (3) do I have improvement room when called? After three questions, build a balanced x/r range.
l4sd-preflop-ranges: Short-Deck Preflop Ranges: Starting-Hand Value Reshuffled

In the 36-card short-deck environment, starting-hand values are reshuffled: pocket pairs rise (trips rank high, 17.6% hit probability), AK is the strongest non-pair but doesn't beat pairs, and suited connectors play well but are secondary. Short-deck preflop ranges therefore favor "pairs and suited hands, with offsuit big high cards relatively devalued".
Short-deck preflop range rule: pairs (including small pairs) and suited hands first; AK secondary; offsuit AX relatively devalued. Build ranges with more combos allocated to pairs/suited connectors.

Short-deck preflop opening tiers: (1) top tier — AA/KK/QQ (pair value high, dominating AK); (2) secondary value — JJ-TT/AK (strongest non-pair); (3) speculative tier — 99-22 (set mining, trips value) / suited connectors JTs+ / suited Ax. Compared with standard hold'em, small pairs and suited connectors carry more weight while offsuit AX drops in relative value.

Example: Short deck, BTN opens and you (BB) hold T♠9♠. T9s is in the speculative tier of short-deck ranges — it can make flushes (beating full houses) and straights, playing well. Against the BTN's ~60% opening range T9s has decent equity and big postflop potential — a standard call. Holding A♠K♦ (offsuit) instead puts it in secondary value — it can make top pair, but with high flop pair density, top-pair value is below standard hold'em.

Example 2 (3Bet range): Short deck, you face a BTN open and consider a 3Bet. The 3Bet range splits into value (JJ+/AK) and bluff (blocker-bearing hands like A5s — blocking AA/AK, folding cleanly to a 4Bet). Short-deck pair density is high, so the 3Bet value layer should carry more pairs (pairs > AK).

Counterintuitive point: in short deck AK isn't a "slight coin-flip favorite" strong shove. It dominates all non-pairs and can flop top pair, but preflop all-in it trails any pocket pair about 43%-45%. Treating AK as a top-tier strong hand is the biggest standard-hold'em-inertia misjudgment.

Short-deck preflop range quick memory: top pairs (AA/KK/QQ) + secondary AK + speculative pairs/suited connectors. Open about 50%-60% (BTN), pairs and suited hands first. Facing a 3Bet, tighten small pairs and suited connectors (speculative value needs implied odds).
l4sd-nuts-equity: The core equity calculation adjustment in short deck is recalculating outs on 36 cards (9 per suit). Flush-draw outs = 9 − seen cards of that suit, and single-street hit rate is estimated by "outs ÷ 33". Short-deck outs are absolutely lower, but made-hand value is high (flushes/straights are often nuts), so chasing nut draws has excellent implied odds.
Short-deck equity rule: recalculate outs on 36 cards (flush = 9 − seen cards of that suit), but made-hand value is high (flush beats full house) → chasing nut draws has excellent implied odds.
Short-Deck Equity Correction and Made-Hand Probability

Short-deck outs and equity correction:

Flush-draw outs = 9 − seen cards of that suit (holding 2 + 2 on board → 5)
Single-street hit rate = outs ÷ 33 (after the flop)

Example: flush draw 5 outs → 5/33 ≈ 15% single-street, about 28% two-street
Straight draw 8 outs → 8/33 ≈ 24% single-street, about 44% two-street

The 2/4 rule on 36 cards: "outs × 2" for one street is more accurate; outs×4 for two streets overestimates.

Made-hand value: flushes (beat full houses) / straights are often nuts → excellent implied odds when chasing. (Concept from: Short Deck Poker outs and equity)

Short-deck equity practice: although short-deck draw equity is absolutely lower than full ring (fewer outs), made-hand value is high — flushes/straights are often nut-tier. So chasing nut draws (flushes/straights) has excellent implied odds and both calls and semi-bluffs are profitable. The key is using short-deck-corrected outs, not the full-ring outs table.

Example: Short deck, you hold A♥K♥ on a 9♥7♥2♣ flop. You draw to the flush: seen hearts A♥K♥ + 9♥7♥ = 4, so flush outs = 9 − 4 = 5. The opponent bets half pot and you need 25%. Your 5 flush outs are 15% single-street but about 28% two-street, and a made flush is the nuts (beats full houses). Adding implied odds (extract a big pot when made), the call is +EV and even a raise-semi-bluff is worth considering.

Example 2 (nut chase): Short deck, you hold 8♠9♠ on a 6♦7♣2♥ flop. You draw to 5 or T for a straight (8 outs; 6/7 seen, 5/T have 4 each = 8). This straight (5-6-7-8-9 or 6-7-8-9-T) is a strong short-deck straight, losing only to full houses/flushes/trips. About 44% two-street and near-nuts when made — both calls and semi-bluffs are excellent.

Counterintuitive point: short-deck flush draws have only 5 outs (full ring 9) and absolutely lower equity — but the made hand is nut-tier (beats full houses), basically locking the pot once made. "Few outs" doesn't mean "weak draw"; the key is the relative strength when made.

Short-deck equity quick math: flush 5 outs ≈ 15% single-street, 28% two-street; straight 8 outs ≈ 24% single-street, 44% two-street. Memorize these, then combine with "made hands are nuts" to judge whether to chase.
l4sd-blocker-bluff: Short-Deck Blockers: Value in a Dense Strong-Hand Environment

A blocker is a card you hold that reduces specific opponent combos. Blocker value is amplified in short deck: because flush value is enormous (beats full houses) and pair density is high, blocking the opponent's flush/pair combos impacts bluffing and calling decisions more. Holding A♠ completely blocks the opponent's A♠X♠ nut flush — extremely valuable in short deck.

Short-deck blocker rule: holding an A blocks the nut flush (opponent's A♥X♥ combos = 0); holding a pair blocks the opponent's pairs. Short-deck flushes/pairs are valuable, so blocking them massively impacts bluff success.

Short-deck blocker-bluff applications: (1) bluff blocking — holding A♠ zeros the opponent's A♠X♠ nut flush, raising bluff success; (2) preflop 3Bet selection — holding an A blocks AA/AK, lowering the 4Bet probability. Short-deck flush/pair value is high, so these blocking effects are amplified and bluff selections should prefer blocker-bearing hands.

Example: Short-deck flop K♠9♠4♠ (three spades), you hold A♦A♣ (no spade A). You block no flushes — the opponent can have the A♠X♠ nut flush or a smaller flush. Your AA's bluff-catching value drops; lean fold. Conversely, holding A♠ (no flush made) blocks every A♠X♠ nut-flush combo and the opponent's "strongest hand" is falsified — your bluff or call success rises.

Example 2 (preflop blocking): Short deck, you (BB) face a BTN open and consider a 3Bet bluff. The difference between A♦5♦ and 7♦6♦: A5s's A blocks the opponent's AA and AK (fewer top hands, lower 4Bet probability) and folds cleanly to a 4Bet; 76s blocks no strong hands and runs into QQ+ more often when 4Bet. Short-deck pair density is high, so the A blocker is more valuable.

Counterintuitive point: short-deck blockers are a marginal tool, not a master key. Holding A♠ raises bluff success but doesn't guarantee it; using it to overturn base range analysis is abuse. Its value in short deck is large (high flush/pair value) but remains "icing after the base range is right".

Short-deck blocker quick memory: on a three-suited board holding A♠ → blocks the nut flush, bonus for bluffing/calling; holding a pair → blocks the opponent's pairs. Off-the-table drill: set up random three-suited boards and count the difference in "opponent nut-flush combos" with and without your A♠.
l4sd-gto-fundamentals: Short-Deck GTO: Adapting the Game Tree and Frequencies

The core difference between short-deck GTO and standard hold'em lies in game-tree structure and made-hand distribution: high pair density, huge flush value, and common draws lead to higher equilibrium betting frequencies, clearer polarization, and larger sizes. Understanding these differences is the prerequisite for applying short-deck GTO.

Short-deck GTO's positioning is a "bulletproof vest": it guarantees you're not exploited but doesn't promise maximum profit. Against a leaky opponent, targeted exploitation earns more — at the cost of opening your own leaks. HU pros switch between "wearing the vest" and "switching to the knife".

Short-deck value:bluff ratio and MDF (formulas unchanged, inputs adjusted):

Value:bluff ratio = b/(1+2b)
Full pot: 1/3 bluffs (2:1)
Half pot: 1/4 bluffs (3:1)

MDF = 1/(1+b): half pot defend 67%, full pot 50%

Short-deck adjustment points:
1. Higher made-hand value (flushes/straights) → value bets can use bigger sizes
2. Draws common → bluff density can be slightly higher (semi-bluff with strong draws)
3. High pair density → defense ranges contain more pairs, supporting higher MDF

Concept from: Short Deck Poker GTO frequencies and 6+ structure

Short-deck GTO practice: because flushes/straights are highly valuable and draws common, short-deck betting ranges are more polarized (strong made hands + semi-bluff draws) and sizes can be larger (big bets extract made-hand value). But frequency balance remains core — value:bluff ratios and defensive MDF must be sound, or the opponent counters you.

Example: Short-deck river full-pot bet, equilibrium value:bluff ratio 2:1. You mix a flush (value) with a missed straight draw (bluff). If you only bet flushes (0% bluffs), the opponent folds everything to your full-pot bets and exploits you; if you bluff more than half, he calls everything and exploits you. The equilibrium ratio leaves the opponent torn.

Example 2 (minimum necessary deviation): You observe a short-deck opponent who calls big river bets only 25% (equilibrium ~50%). Based on this you can raise your river overbet-bluff frequency overall — but capped at "I still don't lose if he corrects to 40%". That's "using GTO as the baseline and making disciplined deviations from observable biases".

Counterintuitive point: short-deck GTO isn't "playing tight" but "keeping everything at ratios the opponent can't counter". Short-deck GTO is full of high-frequency betting, overbet shoves, and semi-bluffs — equilibrium frequencies just look more "aggressive" because made-hand value is high and draws are common.

Short-deck GTO learning path: first use a solver to understand the equilibrium "shape", then use node locking to study "harvest schemes for common opponent leaks", finally validate live. The baseline gives you invincibility; deviations give you profit.
l4sd-solver-readout: Short-Deck Solvers: Methodology for Reading Output

A solver approximates the short-deck equilibrium through iteration, outputting each hand's action frequency and size at every node. Short-deck solver results differ from standard hold'em (more polarized ranges, bigger sizes, more semi-bluffs). The key to reading them isn't memorizing frequencies but understanding "why".

Reading short-deck solvers — three questions: why this sizing on this board? Why is this hand in the betting range? Why did the frequency change on the turn? Understand the structure and the frequencies remember themselves.

Common features of short-deck solver outputs: (1) betting ranges more polarized — strong made hands + strong-draw semi-bluffs, middle hands check; (2) sizes on the big side — 2/3+ pot on wet boards to protect made hands; (3) high semi-bluff frequency — flush/straight draws are valuable and retain improvement room when called. Recognizing these features lets you convert solver outputs into live strategy.

Example: A short-deck solver on a 9♦8♣3♥ flop (wet) outputs: overpairs (KK/QQ) bet 2/3+ pot to protect, A-high and small/medium pairs check, straight/flush draws mix semi-bluff bets. Distill into: on wet boards big-bet protect strong made hands, semi-bluff draws, check middle hands. That's converting the solver into executable strategy.

Example 2 (turn frequency change): A short-deck solver lowers firing frequency when the turn completes the opponent's draws (a flush/straight card). Distill into: when the turn/river changes hands, even if you're ahead, lower betting frequency — because the combos beating you in his range have multiplied.

Counterintuitive point: a solver isn't an "answer" but a "coordinate system". Memorizing solver frequencies gets forgotten; understanding structure transfers to different boards. The mark of a short-deck pro is "using the solver to understand why", not "copying what it does".

Five-step solver reading: (1) look at the betting-range structure (value/semi-bluff/check ratios); (2) look at the size distribution (why this size); (3) look at street changes (how frequencies shift on the turn/river); (4) distill one reusable principle; (5) validate live. Each board read makes your short-deck framework more complete.
l5sd-bankroll: Short-Deck Bankroll Management: The Necessity of High Variance

Short-deck variance is significantly higher than standard hold'em (flop rate/draws/big pots), so bankroll management must be more conservative. Standard hold'em cash needs about 50-100 buy-ins; short deck suggests ≥150. Reason: short-deck standard deviation is higher (all-in equity often lands in 45%-55%), requiring a bigger buffer to survive variance and let expectation converge.
Short-deck bankroll rule: ≥150 buy-ins (higher standard deviation). Bankroll is your survival buffer against short-deck variance; ignoring discipline, short-term swings will break you.

Short-deck bankroll move-up/down rules:

Move up: bankroll reaches 2× the current stake's buy-in count (e.g. 150 buy-ins → move to the 75-buy-in stake)
Move down: bankroll drops below the current stake's buy-in count (e.g. 75 buy-ins → drop to the 150-buy-in stake)

Example: playing the 5-ante stake needs 150×5 = 750 ante of bankroll;
bankroll grows to 1500 ante → consider the 10-ante stake;
bankroll drops below 750 ante → move back down

Discipline: move up slowly (2× before moving), move down fast (drop the moment the line breaks). (Concept from: short-deck high-variance bankroll framework)

Short-deck bankroll practice: move up slowly, move down fast. Because short-deck variance is large, a single downswing can consume 20-30 buy-ins; an insufficient buffer forces you to move down at the worst time. Also follow the "stop and restart" discipline — pause at the budget point instead of chasing and re-buying.

Example: Short deck, you bring 150 buy-ins (1500 ante) to the 10-ante stake. One session loses 30 buy-ins (300 ante) — not yet below the line but close to the variance budget. Correct play: pause for review, not "one more game to get even". Short-deck variance is large; one chase can lose even more in a row.

Example 2 (moving-down discipline): Short deck, your bankroll drops below 75 buy-ins (750 ante). Even if "the table is good", discipline says move down to a smaller stake to rebuild. Short-deck players most often raise to chase when under-bankrolled — a dangerous violation of bankroll discipline.

Counterintuitive point: the hardest part of short-deck bankroll management is "moving up too fast while winning". Winning a few buy-ins then jumping stakes puts you in bigger variance. Short deck moves up slowly (2× bankroll) and down fast.

Short-deck bankroll triad: (1) ≥150 buy-ins; (2) move up at 2×, move down the moment the line breaks; (3) pause and review at the variance budget — don't chase and re-buy. Hold these three and variance won't break you.
l5sd-tilt-control: Short-Deck Emotion Control: The Challenge of High Variance

Short deck is a tilt hotspot: high variance, big pots, violent win-loss alternation. Tilt in short deck comes from result dependence, dashed expectations, and revenge psychology, and triggers more easily because losing streaks are common (45%-55% all-ins). Tilt distorts your range (opening looser, calling wider, chasing harder), systematically deviating from baseline.

Short-deck tilt-defense triad: self-awareness (emotional red light), preset discipline (stop-loss point), process attribution (only ask EV). Build the defenses off the table so they're ready when tilt hits.

Recognizing short-deck downswings: losing multiple 45%-55% all-ins in a row is mathematical normalcy (0.5^8 ≈ 0.4%), but short deck has frequent all-ins per hour, so downswings arrive faster. After recognition, distinguish "mathematical variance" from "strategy errors" — record each key decision's reasoning in a decision log, asking only EV not results. Discipline training: preset the stop-loss, leave at the line, review only process.

Example: Short deck, you lose 6 consecutive 50% all-ins (0.5^6 ≈ 1.6%, encountered several times an hour in short deck). Your mind knows "I played right" but emotions want "to get even". If you size up to chase losses, that's a tilt loop. The right move: recognize the revenge impulse → pause 10 minutes → restart with "what is this hand's EV".

Example 2 (process vs result): Short deck, you shove AK vs 55 (short-deck AK vs 55 ≈ 43%-45%) and 55 wins. You lost the result, but the process: with proper pot odds, calling was +EV — you played right. Short-deck pros review only process: "was this decision EV-correct?" Tilters review only results: "I lost to junk again."

Counterintuitive point: the most dangerous tilt in short deck isn't "impulse when losing" but "letting your guard down after winning". After winning a few hands, players relax, play marginal hands, and give the edge back. Short-deck discipline must be consistent throughout, win or lose.

Short-deck tilt-control triad: (1) emotional red light — pause after N consecutive hands wanting revenge; (2) preset stop-loss — leave after losing 40-50BB; (3) process attribution — review only EV. Build all three off the table so they're ready when tilt hits.
l6sd-tourney-i: Short-Deck MTT: Chip Rhythm and Survival

Short-deck MTT (multi-table tournaments) differs from cash: blinds rise over time, chips are a finite resource, and ICM pressure dominates. Short-deck tournament chip rhythm: deep-stack stages (50BB+) can maintain cash-style play; shallow-stack stages (under 20BB) shift to preflop shove games. Short-deck's high variance makes tournament survival strategy even more important.

Short-deck MTT golden rule: the shallower your stack and the higher the blind share, the more frequent preflop shoves. Short-deck variance is high, so tournaments must balance "survival" and "aggression", avoiding unnecessary variance.

Short-deck MTT chip rhythm by stage: (1) deep stacks (50BB+) — cash-style play, wide ranges, more postflop; (2) medium stacks (20-50BB) — min-raise + postflop; (3) short stacks (under 20BB) — preflop shoves dominate. Because short-deck variance is high, in shallow stages you should actively shove with equity to steal blinds and double up.

Example: Short-deck MTT medium stack, you hold A♠Q♠ and the opponent (BB) 3Bets. AQ is secondary value in short deck (non-pair but strong). Facing a 3Bet, look at stack depth and opponent tendencies: deep-stacked call to see postflop; shallow-stacked (under 20BB) shove directly (AQ has good equity vs a wide range). Chip rhythm decides how the same hand is played.

Example 2 (survival strategy): Short-deck MTT bubble, you (BB) hold K♦Q♠ facing a BTN shove. Short-deck KQ is a non-pair, about 35%-40% vs the BTN's shoving range (pairs/strong Ax). Under bubble ICM pressure, a healthy stack leans fold to survive; a short stack calls to double. Short-deck tournaments balance survival and aggression.

l7sd-deep-stack: Short-Deck Deep Stacks: Value Extraction and Nut Confrontation

The core of short-deck deep-stack (100BB+) strategy is value extraction and nut confrontation: flushes/straights are highly valuable, so deep-stacked you must fire three barrels to extract full value; meanwhile deep stacks amplify RIO (reverse implied odds), making marginal made hands more easily dominated — pot control and stop-loss.

Short-deck deep-stack rule: strong made hands (flushes/straights/two pair) fire three barrels for value; marginal made hands pot-control and stop-loss (deep stacks amplify RIO). Use big sizes so the pot grows geometrically and the river shove lands.

Short-deck deep stacks (high SPR): strong made hands need big sizes (2/3+ pot) so the pot grows geometrically street by street and the river shove extracts value. Meanwhile, in nut confrontation — short-deck flush/straight value is high, so deep-stacked you should actively build the pot, letting the opponent's weak made hands (top pair/two pair) call your nuts.

Example: Short deck, 150BB deep, you (BTN) hold A♥K♥ on a 9♥7♥2♣ flop with a flush draw. Turn 5♥ — you make the flush! You have the nut flush (beats full houses). Deep-stacked, use big bets to extract — flop 2/3 pot, big turn bet, river overbet or shove — letting the opponent's top pair/two pair call your nut flush. Short-deck flush value is high; deep-stacked value extraction is maximized.

Example 2 (marginal made-hand control): Short deck, deep-stacked, you hold A♠Q♠ on a Q♦9♣8♠ flop (top pair + straight-draw board). Deep-stacked top pair has high RIO (the opponent may have 9x/8x/straight draws) — pot control and stop-loss, small bets or checks, avoiding a big pot then getting outdrawn. Deep stacks amplify RIO, so marginal made hands must be conservative.

Counterintuitive point: deep-stacked short deck makes the contrast between "fast-play strong hands" and "pot-control marginal hands" more extreme. Deep stacks amplify both made-hand value (strong hands extract more) and RIO (marginal hands lose more) — go to both extremes.

Short-deck deep-stack quick memory: strong made hands fire three barrels for extraction (river shove); marginal made hands pot-control and stop-loss. At high SPR, every street first ask "is my hand nut-tier or marginal", then decide extract or control.
l7sd-shallow-stack: Short-Deck Shallow Stacks: The Push/Fold Game

The core of short-deck shallow-stack (under 30BB) strategy is the Push/Fold (shove/fold) game: complex postflop play fails, and preflop shoves become the main weapon. Short-deck's high variance makes shallow-stack strategy more extreme — actively shove with equity to steal and double, because waiting costs more (high blind share and short-deck draws flop often).
Short-deck shallow-stack rule: under 30BB preflop shoves dominate; use any hand with equity (pairs/Ax/strong suited connectors) to steal and double. Complex postflop play fails at shallow stacks.

Short-deck shallow-stack Push/Fold break-even (shove S ante, pot blinds):

EV(shove) = f×Pot − (1−f)×[S × (1−E_win) − E_win × (Pot + S)]
(f = opponent fold rate, E_win = equity when called)

Example: you shove 15 ante, pot 3 ante, opponent folds 40%, your KQs equity when called 45%:
EV = 0.4×3 − 0.6×[15×0.55 − 0.45×18] = 1.2 − 0.6×[8.25 − 8.1] = 1.2 − 0.09 = 1.11

Short-deck shallow-stack KQs shove EV is positive — backed by fold rate + equity when called. (Concept from: short-deck Push/Fold math)

Short-deck shallow-stack Push/Fold practice: the shoving range has two layers — value (pairs/strong Ax, ahead when called) + bluff/semi-bluff (strong suited connectors, fold rate + improvement room when called). Short-deck pair density is high, so shallow-stack pair shoves carry more value. Avoid shoving weak offsuit hands (trailing pairs when called).

Example: Short deck, shallow 15BB, you (BTN) hold K♠Q♠. KQs has about 45% equity vs the BB's calling range (pairs/strong Ax), plus fold rate (the BB may fold weak hands) — the 15BB shove is +EV. Short-deck shallow-stack KQs is a standard shove — backed by fold rate + equity when called.

Short-deck shallow stacks must avoid shoving weak offsuit hands.

Counterintuitive point: "wait for good cards" is wrong at short-deck shallow stacks. The blind share is high, waiting costs a lot, and short-deck draws flop often — actively shoving with equity (pairs/Ax/strong suited connectors) is the correct answer. Only weak offsuit hands fold.

Short-deck shallow-stack quick memory: under 15BB shoves dominate; shoving range = pairs/Ax (value) + strong suited connectors (semi-bluff); avoid weak offsuit shoves. First count your stack (in BBs), then decide Push or Fold.
l8sd-exploit-i: Short-Deck Exploitation: Recreational Players' Cognitive Biases

Most short-deck recreational players come from standard hold'em carrying full-ring cognitive biases: wrong outs, underrated flushes, overrated AK, set-mining too loosely. Short-deck exploitation is about identifying these biases and harvesting with targeted strategies. Identification relies on 50-100 hand frequency statistics, not single-hand impressions.

Short-deck exploitation rule: identify the opponent's "standard hold'em inertia" (wrong outs / underrated flushes / overrated AK) and harvest with targeted strategies. Aim at the leak with minimal magnitude, returning to baseline when the opponent adjusts.

Short-deck exploitation has two levers: (1) range exploitation — after identifying that the opponent chases too loosely (wrong outs) or misorders value (underrated flushes), adjust your value/bluffs accordingly; (2) bet sizing — when the opponent underrates flushes, your flush value bets can be bigger; when he chases too loosely, your protection bets can be bigger. Frequency statistics back each adjustment.

Example: You notice the opponent chases with the full-ring outs table (flush as 9 outs; short deck is 5). His chases are too loose and his actual equity is overestimated. Exploit: your value bets can be bigger and your calls tighter — his chases are expensive and rarely get there. After recognizing this cognitive bias you can extract targeted value.

Example 2 (underrating flushes): The opponent uses standard hold'em rankings and thinks full house > flush. When you make a flush and he makes a full house, he mistakenly thinks the full house is bigger and keeps calling your big bets. Exploit: on flush boards (which beat full houses) your value bets can be more aggressive because he misjudges strength.

Counterintuitive point: "the opponent using full-ring intuition" is the most exploitable leak in short deck. Their outs are wrong, their hand rankings are wrong, and their starting-hand values are overestimated — these biases make your value bets more valuable and your calls more profitable. Identifying biases matters more than memorizing more GTO.

Short-deck exploitation quick memory: watch four signals in opponents — do they chase with short-deck outs, misjudge strength on flush boards, shove AK too often, or set-mine too loosely? Each signal maps to an exploitation direction.
l8sd-exploit-ii: Short-Deck Exploitation (II): The Dynamic Game of High Variance

Short-deck's high variance makes exploitation a dynamic game: variance is large, win-loss alternates fast, and opponents adjust frequently. Short-deck exploitation (II) focuses on using table dynamics (who's tilting, who's deep, who's passive) and targeted counter-responses (returning to baseline when the opponent adjusts). Exploitation isn't one-shot but a "deviate → get detected → return to baseline" loop.

Short-deck dynamic exploitation rule: identify table dynamics (tilt/stack/passivity), harvest with targeted strategies, and return to the GTO baseline when the opponent adjusts. Exploitation is a dynamic game — aim at the leak with minimal magnitude.
Using Table Dynamics and Targeted Counter-Responses

Short-deck table-dynamic usage: (1) tilting opponents — recognize and pressure aggressively, because they play marginal hands to chase losses; (2) short-stacked opponents — pressure with a wide range because they fear elimination; (3) passive opponents — bet at high frequency because they won't raise back. Targeted counter-responses: when the opponent adjusts against you (e.g. raising his 3Bet frequency), return to the GTO baseline and narrow your range.

Example: Short deck, you notice an opponent starts tilting after consecutive losses — playing marginal hands, mindless chases, losing sizing control. Exploit: value-bet against him with a wider range and call tighter — he over-chases and your value bets get overpaid. Recognizing and harvesting a tilting opponent is a classic short-deck dynamic exploitation.

Example 2 (targeted counter-response): After you raise your steal frequency against an opponent, he starts 3Betting frequently in response — he's discovered your deviation. Now you must return to the GTO baseline (narrow the steal range, reduce pure bluffs), or your newly opened leaks get harvested in reverse. Exploitation is a dynamic game: deviate → get detected → return to baseline.

Example 3 (short-stack pressure): Short deck, you're deep (100 ante) vs a short stack (30 ante). The short stack fears elimination, so you shove/raise with a wide range to pressure — his ICM pressure keeps him from risking. Short-deck's high variance makes deep-stack pressure on shorts more effective.

Counterintuitive point: the biggest risk of short-deck dynamic exploitation is "over-exploiting and becoming the leak yourself". When you identify the opponent's adjustment, you must return to baseline — short-deck/HU pros always keep one hand on the GTO baseline wheel while harvesting.

Short-deck dynamic exploitation in five steps: (1) identify table dynamics (who's tilting / who's short / who's passive); (2) adjust against the leak (pressure/value/counter); (3) observe the opponent's reaction; (4) return to baseline when he adjusts; (5) re-check every 500 hands. A dynamic game, advanced in loops.
